newsitem.title: BURUNDI: FEATURE-Burundi army trains to fight after coup.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Burundi army trains to fight after coup.

text.p: Burundi's mainly Tutsi army says it has no shortage of recruits to join the battle against Hutu rebels fighting to bring down the government it put in place.
About 1,000 novices train in the morning sun, some drilling in companies, others doing fitness training.
The young soldiers, whom the instructors say are mostly about 18 years old, are dressed in green shirts and blue camouflage pants held up by brass-buckled belts.
Boots are in short supply, and only those who make it into the real ranks -- after about three months of training -- will be given them. In the meantime the recruits wear track shoes.
An army colonel watching the recruits said that some boys sign up from 16, even though many look even younger than that.
An instructor says they are chosen from several thousand more volunteers. Many fell by the wayside, leaving them to join local militias or filling the ranks of the unemployed.
"They want to join up, to be a part. And those left behind are very sad," says one officer, who like the others declined to be quoted by name.
The army refuses to discuss the ethnic make-up of its ranks but African and Western diplomats say Hutus are correct in believing it is overwhelmingly drawn from Burundi's 15 percent Tutsi minority.

A small group of civilians gathers at the side of the field to watch the training and a small boy too young to join up marches behind the instructor before being shooed away in the direction of a military band blaring out a quick march.
The recruits, drawn from the city and neighbouring countryside, have no French or English, the instructor says, declining to act as an interpreter.

Few of the recruits will ever have the education of their commanders. Their colonel, an imposing man in camouflage fatigues, says the officers are taught in as many fields as possible. He trained as a paratrooper, in artillery and military strategy, having begun his studies as an economist.
About 150,000 people, mainly civilians, have been killed in three years of fighting and massacres in Burundi. The army blames Hutu rebels and civilian extremists.
The rebels and many Hutus say the Tutsi minority's dream of supremacy, backed by their army, is at fault.
The army, which seized power on July 25 after throwing out ethnic Hutu President Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, says it is there to be a force for the whole country, not just a section.
"The army is there to protect Tutsis and Hutus," said military spokesman Lieutenant-Colonel Longin Minani who accuses the rebels of waging war on civilians.
"What we are having in Burundi is not a political struggle, it is an ideology of genocide," he says.
But an aid worker says Hutus have suffered gross human rights violations at the hands of the army, which he says is clearly dominated by Tutsis.

"(Hutus) are against Buyoya and the military. They are afraid. There has been no justice," the aid worker says, adding that the army drove Hutus out of Bujumbura's Kamenge suburb last year and were now trying to clear Hutus from the hills above the capital, already dubbed "Tutsiville".
One colonel says the national army is about 25,000 strong, but no one really knows how many armed people it is fighting against.
The military says sanctions slapped on the landlocked country in retaliation for the army coup on July 25 only help the rebels, free to move in Burundi's western neighbour Zaire.
Another humanitarian worker says in Burundi the future is grim: the country has the highest population density in Africa and land is scarce.
"There are a lot of young (Tutsi) fellows who sign up. Others, (Hutus) are taken by press-gangs of rebels.... Many mothers just think that their sons are doomed," she says.
